donnees.titre: Long-Term Inhaled Corticosteroid Use and the Risk of Open-Angle Glaucoma in Patients with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease.
donnees.revue: International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
donnees.resume:
PURPOSE: The question of whether inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) increase the risk of open-angle glaucoma (OAG) has produced conflicting data on short-term effects, but no study has evaluated their long-term effects. We assessed whether long-term cumulative ICS use is associated with an increased risk of incident OAG among patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: The United Kingdom Clinical Practice Research Datalink was used to form a cohort of patients with COPD, aged 40 years or more, who initiated an inhaled maintenance treatment, between September 2013 and March 2021. Subjects were followed until the occurrence of the first OAG diagnosis. Using a nested case-control design, each OAG case was matched with up to 100 concurrently glaucoma-free controls using risk-set sampling. Conditional logistic regression was used to compute the adjusted odds ratio of incident OAG associated with cumulative ICS exposure, as an estimate of the hazard ratio (HR) and its 95% confidence interval (CI).
RESULTS: The COPD cohort included 84,564 subjects, with 732 developing OAG (incidence rate 2.64 per 1000 person-years) and 56% having used an ICS since cohort entry. The adjusted HR of OAG associated with any ICS use since cohort entry, compared with non-use, was 1.14 (95% CI, 0.94-1.38). The HR was 1.11 (95% CI, 0.83-1.48) for total cumulative dose ≥365 mg and 1.23 (95% CI, 0.90-1.68) for over 3 years since ICS initiation.
CONCLUSION: This large cohort study did not observe a statistically significant increase in the risk of OAG with ICS use, including long-term use and higher cumulative doses, among patients with COPD.
